i met the oldest person in the world today.

here’s what he told me about how to live
a long, healthy life (tldr at the end):

josé flores was born on July 11, 1907, he is 119 years old.

“what's the secret to living 119 years?”, i asked him…

“trabajo!” (work)

up until a few years ago, José was still on his farm, planting crops and chopping brush with a machete.

in Japan, they call this Ikigai (生き甲斐), a word meaning “a reason for being.” It is well known to be associated with longevity across many cultures. (pmid 19539820)

his lifestyle defies most mainstream longevity ideas...

-he doesn't fear the sun. He works in it daily.

-he eats meat every single day: beef, fish, or chicken, & organs like heart and liver. nothing from the animal is wasted.

(large population studies corroborate the strong, consistent association between animal food consumption and longevity. (pmid 35228814))

-he eats local foods & doesn’t fear natural sugars. Fruit, vegetables, milk, and honey.

-he cooks with animal fats and adds these to staples like rice and beans. lard, tallow, and butter.

he doesn’t fear saturated fat, nor do most in this nicoya region of costa rica.

-he doesn't drink coffee (!) , but he loves young coconut water & agua dulce- a juice made from sugar cane.

-he plays dominoes every day with his family and visitors to keep his mind sharp.

the formula for maxing out your genetic longevity potential doesn’t have to be complex or cost thousands of dollars:

i. eat unprocessed food.

single ingredient foods (meat, plants, with no ingredient labels) for >95% of meals.

ii. find a purpose, and work toward it daily.

iii. get outside. don't fear the sun.

moderate exposure is associated with longevity in many studies (PMID 26992108)

iv. stay close to your people.

the people you care about are critical to the formula. Protect that community.

a large study from Harvard found that meaningful community was the strongest predictor of longevity. (PMID 31495897)

v. don't take life too seriously. Laugh as much as possible.

everyone I have met in my exploration of longevity (ikaria, sardinia, nicoya, switzerland…) who was aging well had an easy sense of humor and smiled + laughed often.

tldr:

longevity doesn’t have to be as complicated as it’s made out to be.

high food quality with animal foods
moderate sunlight
movement
purpose
community

eat food for humans, live like a human, & thrive.

we all have a genetic longevity potential, this is how you maximize it.

Maintaining a clear mind is the hardest challenge of life. 

By default we settle into patterns. We do what's easily available and pattern match what others do. 

Getting swept away by the day which turn into years. Awaking one day and wondering what even happened to the time. 

I've found my morning routine is the best antidote to becoming the System. That is, unthinkingly becoming the default patterns that dominate your era. 

Each day, it's time without screens, messages, scrolling, interruptions, and social pressures. 

It's filled with silence, the discomfort of discipline and the open space of thought. 

There is something magical about the morning. A time when life is reborn each day. I find my greatest solace and joy in them. 

p.s. those of you with kids, I hear you. I have three children. Morning routines are practically impossible. Hang in there and even if it's a 15 minute routine, it can be a good practice to maintain sanity amid the chaos.
hits.draft_en:
Bryan Johnson reckons keeping a clear head is the hardest job going.

Left alone, we fall into the same patterns as everyone else. Do what's easy, copy what's around us, and the days roll into years before you notice.

And he's honest about it: with kids, a full routine is near impossible. Even 15 minutes counts.

For blokes on early starts, that might be ten minutes with a cuppa before the phone comes out. Small, but it's yours.

Your fat used to be mostly animal. Now it’s mostly soybean.

In 1960, about 13% of American adults were obese. Today it’s ~40%. Severe obesity went from under 1% to nearly 10%.
That’s the quantity. The composition changed even more quietly.

A 2015 review of U.S. adipose tissue samples found linoleic acid (the main fat in seed oils) rose from ~9% of stored fat in 1959 to ~21.5% by 2008 — a 136% increase. It tracked dietary linoleic acid intake almost perfectly as soybean oil flooded the food supply.

Your grandparents’ fat cells were built from butter, lard, and tallow. Yours are built from the industrial oils that replaced them. 

Those oils are more prone to oxidation, more integrated into cell membranes, and part of the same dietary environment that also delivered the refined carbs and ultra-processed calories that expanded the total fat mass.

More fat. Different fat. Same timeframe as the obesity epidemic.

Even with a perfect diet, the combination of many things –including our depleted soils, the storage and transportation of our food, genetic alterations of traditional heirloom species, and the increased stress and nutritional demands resulting from a toxic environment – make it impossible for us to get the vitamins and minerals we need solely from the foods we eat.

Emerging scientific evidence shows the importance of nutrients as essential helpers in our biochemistry and metabolism. They are the oil that greases the wheels of our metabolism. Be sure to pick quality supplements. Think of them as part of your diet. You want the best-quality food and the best-quality supplements you can buy.

Prader-Willi syndrome. Hyperphagia and the measures required to contain it.

The hypothalamus never signals fullness.
Food-seeking continues until the stomach fails.

Standard response in the literature and parent accounts: external barriers.
Padlocked refrigerators and cabinets.
Kitchen doors locked or gated.
Food moved to high shelves or sibling rooms with their own locks.

Motion alarms. Cameras. Keys hidden under mattresses (retrieved at night by crawling in).

•  Families report children who pick locks with bobby pins, unscrew door hinges, or raid garbage and school cafeterias.
•  Mothers describe installing heavy garden gates after a child bypassed five successive stair gates.
•  Adult children themselves request that the fridge and pantry stay locked because the constant drive is more tolerable when the option is physically removed.
When those barriers fail, the stomach can rupture.

For anyone who has experienced significant medical trauma, talking about it can be incredibly difficult. Even in private circles, let alone publicly.

Add to that the shame and embarrassment of having a condition that leaves you literally shitting blood, withdrawing from social situations, and watching your physical decline hurt the people you love.

It's an incredibly painful thing to talk about.

And for me, the hardest part was watching what it did to my parents.

I was the oldest child. I was supposed to set the example.

I'd done everything right on paper to make them and my family proud, to make the most of the support and investment they'd given me. I was valedictorian of my college, had a full scholarship to Oxford, and a place at Harvard Medical School.

And yet, all that promise seemed to be slipping away as I found myself in and out of the hospital.

I remember my mom flying over from Boston to the UK.

There I was, lying in a hospital bed, emaciated and depleted, watching tears roll down her face as she tried to comfort me.

I still haven't let go of that image.

Even writing about it brings me tremendous pain and shame.

So yes, when I'm struggling to communicate about these experiences (and I won't pretend I'm perfect at it) I sometimes put my foot in my mouth. Sometimes I articulate things in ways that reflect how I'm trying to cope with what happened.

Cuy is just meat. The rest is cultural conditioning.
In the Andes, guinea pigs (cuy) have been raised as livestock for over 5,000 years—domesticated long before the Inca and long before Europeans arrived. They weren’t pets. •  ~19–20% protein
•  Very low fat (often cited around 1.6%)
•  Solid mineral content (iron, zinc, phosphorus)
•  Easy to digest, high biological value protein

Cato the Elder wrote De Agri Cultura (~160 BCE), a practical farm manual that treated slave food as a management tool, not charity.
He prescribed fixed rations by role and season:
•  Field hands: 4 modii of wheat in winter, 4.5 in summer.
•  Chain-gang workers: 4 pounds of bread in winter, rising to 5 during peak vineyard work, then back to 4.
•  Overseers, housekeepers, and shepherds: less.
•  Wine scaled by month (thin “after-wine” after harvest, more later), plus salt, windfall olives or fish-paste, and oil.
The overseer was told to keep slaves from hunger and cold so they wouldn’t steal or slack, but also to keep them constantly busy. Extra food only when labor intensity rose. When sick, rations were cut.
The system was deliberate: enough calories and bulk for hard work, issued in coarse, controlled portions that reinforced dependence and limited surplus. Productivity and order were the metrics, not abundance or autonomy.

Off the southwestern coast of Madagascar, near the port of Tulear (now Toliara), a ship went down in a violent storm centuries ago. Every person aboard perished.

Vegans have a substantially higher risk of breaking bones — especially hips.

The EPIC-Oxford study followed nearly 55,000 people in the UK for an average of 18 years and compared fracture rates across diet groups. After adjusting for socioeconomic factors, lifestyle, and body weight, the results were clear:

• Vegans had a 43% higher risk of any fracture compared to meat eaters (HR 1.43).

• Hip fractures were more than double (HR 
2.31) — roughly 15 extra hip fractures for every 1,000 people over 10 years.

• Leg fractures were also about twice as high.

The differences were partly related to lower average BMI, calcium intake, and protein intake in the vegan group, but they remained elevated even after those adjustments. 

In other words, the higher fracture risk wasn’t fully explained by those factors alone.

This is the largest prospective study looking at both total and site-specific fractures in vegans versus meat eaters. 

It doesn’t prove that a vegan diet directly causes weaker bones in every individual, but it does show a consistent, clinically meaningful association in a large, long-running cohort.

Bones need adequate protein, calcium, and sufficient body mass/loading. For many people following a strict vegan diet, those pieces are harder to get in adequate amounts without careful planning and supplementation. The data suggest that, on average, it shows up in fracture rates.

Tong et al., BMC Medicine, 2020.

Bread and circuses, then and now
Juvenal coined panem et circenses in the early 2nd century AD. The people who once granted military commands, high office, and legions had reduced their demands to two things: free grain and public games. 
Rome’s grain dole (the annona) and spectacles at the Circus Maximus and Colosseum kept large numbers of urban citizens fed and distracted. Civic engagement declined as political power concentrated.
Modern versions operate on the same logic:
•  Cheap, abundant calories (subsidized grains, ultra-processed food, SNAP-style programs) replace the grain dole.
•  Always-on entertainment (streaming, sports, social media, reality TV, algorithmic feeds) replaces the circus.
•  Both reduce the time and incentive for sustained attention to policy, institutions, or long-term trade-offs.
The mechanism is unchanged: sufficient comfort and stimulation make higher-order political involvement feel optional. The scale and delivery channels are larger; the underlying exchange is the same.
